q1: SELECT A.PROJECT_ID, ROUND(AVG(B.EXPERIENCE_YEARS), 2) AS AVERAGE_YEARS FROM PROJECT AS A INNER JOIN EMPLOYEE AS B ON A.EMPLOYEE_ID = B.EMPLOYEE_ID GROUP BY A.PROJECT_ID
q2: SELECT PROJECT_ID, ROUND(SUM(EXPERIENCE_YEARS)/COUNT(NAME),2) AS AVERAGE_YEARS FROM PROJECT P JOIN EMPLOYEE E ON P.EMPLOYEE_ID=E.EMPLOYEE_ID GROUP BY PROJECT_ID ORDER BY PROJECT_ID

counterexample: INSERT INTO EMPLOYEE (EMPLOYEE_ID, NAME, EXPERIENCE_YEARS) VALUES (1, 'John', 5), (2, 'John', 3), (3, 'Alice', 4); INSERT INTO PROJECT (PROJECT_ID, EMPLOYEE_ID) VALUES (101, 1), (101, 2), (101, 3);
explanation: Q1 calculates the average experience years for each project by dividing the total experience years of all employees in the project by the number of employees in that project. Q2, on the other hand, calculates the average experience years by dividing the total experience years of all employees in the project by the count of unique employee names in that project. This difference arises because the count of unique employee names might be less than the actual number of employees if there are duplicate names.
counterexample_dsp: The test data should have at least two employees with the same name working on the same project. This will cause Q2 to divide the total experience years by a smaller number (the count of unique names) than Q1 (the actual number of employees), leading to a different average.
